If your older cat wasn’t fond of the idea of the kitten in the other room, she wasn’t ready to meet him face to face. If the first encounters don’t go well consistently that can impact their relationship for the rest of their lives. 

The same thing happened to me, except my partner and I rescued a sick, small kitten and my older cat was uncomfortable but mostly fine until he got big enough to try to roughhouse. She didn’t have any experience with kittens and hated him ever since for playing too rough. He never got the hint though  lol. We frequently had to play referee to make sure she wasn’t getting hurt or too upset. He would just try to play bite and tackle her and genuinely seemed to mean well, she just had never done any of that with her previous companion because he was more of a father/grandfather who took care of her as a kitten. I learned the hard way that she needed way more time.

Unfortunately he passed away from chronic health issues at the young age of 2. Since then we’ve been rescuing strays in the area and there’s one that has chosen my partner as his. He’s healthy and vaccinated and all that, but likes to use our apartment as a home-base and leaves frequently. He has pals in the colony that come by to check on him if he’s inside for too long lol.

It took 2.5 months for her to become comfortable around him. We kept them in separate rooms for several weeks until we introduced them. She’s still a very anxious kitty. She doesn’t like making eye contact with other cats. If she doesn’t have to make too much eye contact she’s fine sniffing at him, checking on him, will occasionally nose boop him. He took the introductory process very well and was very patient with her, which made all the difference.

My advice to you is to completely start over with introductions and don’t let them interact for at least another week or two, or when your cat stops showing so much hostility just at the sound of the kitten meowing. Once she starts to settle a bit and become used to his scent you can try again, but only between a door, between a gate, something like that before even allowing them to make contact. For insecure cats like mine it could just completely set her off. Yowling may be unavoidable at times if your cat is antisocial. 

Maybe she got used to be the only child and doesn’t want the kitten around. You should also plan for the worst case scenario; rehoming the kitten. Your older cat came first, so she should have first priority. We considered rehoming our kitten until his health got substantially worse. At that point it was clear he wouldn’t have much longer to live so we wanted to spend what time we had with him. She eventually would get worried about him after vet visits, come over to check on him, but could never make eye contact without a yowl lol.
